Getting started with deconflate

Source: vignettes/deconflate.Rmd
deconflate.Rmd
library(deconflate)

The problem

Single-disease impact estimates compare animals with and without a disease. Animals with one disease are more (or less) likely to have associated diseases, so each estimate partly reflects the impacts of those other diseases. Adding such estimates double counts. deconflate adjusts (“de-conflates”) the estimates so that they can be aggregated.

The package assumes no species, outcome or unit. The examples use dairy cattle and milk yield, but any population of animals (or people) and any additive outcome works the same way.

A population and an impact table

The population holds what every outcome shares: the disease probabilities and the association rows. This is the three-disease example from the Supplementary File of Rasmussen et al. (2022):

pop <- cm_population(
  cm_diseases(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(0.10, 0.15, 0.20), measure = "prevalence"),
  cm_associations(c("d1", "d1", "d2"), c("d2", "d3", "d3"), c(2, 1, 3), measure = "OR")
)
pop
#> <cm_population>
#>   Diseases: 3 (d1, d2, d3)
#>   Association rows: 3 (OR: 3)
#>   Disease pairs: 3 (3 with a crude pair row, 0 unknown)

Each association row relates a disease to the diseases it is associated_with. Rows are odds ratios by default (risk ratios, risk differences, phi coefficients, prevalences and ratios of odds ratios are also accepted; see ?cm_associations). A row can also be about a combination of diseases, hold within a subgroup (among), be adjusted for other diseases (adjusted_for), and a pair can have several rows (from several studies), which are pooled; see vignette("interactions"). An odds ratio of 1, as for d1 and d3, states that two diseases are unrelated. A pair with no row at all is unknown: deconflate() then fills it in from the other rows (below).

A model adds one impact table: at least one raw estimate per disease, all in the same units. The units can be anything additive (percent of yield, kg of milk, days, euros, a welfare score); the engine does not convert them, and the results come back in the units supplied.

yield <- cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(2.5, 5, 7.5),
                    label = "milk yield loss", units = "% of yield")
m <- cm_model(pop, yield)
m
#> <cm_model>
#>   Diseases: 3 (d1, d2, d3)
#>   Association rows: 3 (OR: 3)
#>   Disease pairs: 3 (3 with a crude pair row, 0 unknown)
#>   Impacts: milk yield loss [% of yield] (additive)
#>   Impact rows: 3 (0 adjusted, 0 within subgroups)

The same impacts in kg give the same adjustment, in kg:

kg <- cm_model(pop, cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(250, 500, 750),
                               units = "kg/animal/year"))
deconflate(kg)$adjusted
#>   disease    kind raw adjusted      change rows
#> 1      d1 disease 250 214.3250 -0.14269981    1
#> 2      d2 disease 500 338.7080 -0.32258408    1
#> 3      d3 disease 750 693.4209 -0.07543874    1

Each deconflate() call adjusts one impact table. For another outcome, make another model on the same population and call deconflate() again:

ci <- cm_model(pop, cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(4, 10, 2),
                               label = "calving interval increase", units = "days"))
deconflate(ci)$adjusted
#>   disease    kind raw  adjusted      change rows
#> 1      d1 disease   4 2.9784447 -0.25538884    1
#> 2      d2 disease  10 9.6989318 -0.03010682    1
#> 3      d3 disease   2 0.3798539 -0.81007307    1

The tables can also be read from CSV files (with any names) or data frames with cm_read_inputs(), which checks them and reports every problem at once (see vignette("own-data")):

ex <- system.file("extdata", "five_diseases", package = "deconflate")
five <- cm_read_inputs(diseases = file.path(ex, "diseases.csv"),
                       associations = file.path(ex, "associations.csv"),
                       impacts = file.path(ex, "impacts_yield.csv"))
five
#> <cm_model>
#>   Diseases: 5 (LAM, MAS, MET, SCK, RP)
#>   Association rows: 12 (OR: 7; OR_ratio: 1; phi: 1; prevalence: 1; RD: 1; RR: 1)
#>   Disease pairs: 10 (10 with a crude pair row, 0 unknown)
#>   Impacts: milk yield loss [% of yield] (additive)
#>   Impact rows: 5 (0 adjusted, 0 within subgroups)
#>   Uncertain inputs (with a distribution): 17

Adjusting impacts 

res <- deconflate(m)
res
#> <cm_result> pairwise shortcut; milk yield loss [% of yield]
#> 
#>  disease raw adjusted   change
#>       d1 2.5    2.143 -0.14270
#>       d2 5.0    3.387 -0.32258
#>       d3 7.5    6.934 -0.07544
#> 
#> Raw sum: 2.5; adjusted total: 2.109
#> Diagnostics: residual 8.88e-16, condition number 1.53, sign changes 0
#> 
#> Notes:
#> * No input has a distribution, so no draws were run: the results are point
#>   estimates.

deconflate() has one model. It describes the population by the maximum-entropy distribution of disease combinations that matches every association row (the distribution that assumes nothing beyond the rows), and finds the adjusted impacts (and any interactions) that reproduce every impact row. Up to 20 diseases it enumerates all combinations; beyond that it uses the sampled backend of fit_joint() (vignette("thresholds-and-scaling")).

When every association row is a crude row about a pair, every pair has one, and every impact row is a crude or adjusted row about one disease, the pairwise 2x2 tables give the same answer as the full distribution, and deconflate() uses them directly (it still fits the distribution once, to check that the rows can hold together). $diagnostics$method says which was used:

res$diagnostics$method
#> [1] "pairwise shortcut"

Leaving out the d1:d3 odds ratio makes that pair unknown:

pop_unknown <- cm_population(pop$diseases,
                             cm_associations(c("d1", "d2"), c("d2", "d3"), c(2, 3)))
res_unknown <- deconflate(cm_model(pop_unknown, yield))
res_unknown$diagnostics$method
#> [1] "full model"
res_unknown$unknown_pairs
#>   disease1 disease2 fitted_or
#> 1       d1       d3  1.143088
rbind(odds_ratio_1 = setNames(res$adjusted$adjusted, res$adjusted$disease),
      unknown = res_unknown$adjusted$adjusted)
#>                    d1       d2       d3
#> odds_ratio_1 2.143250 3.387080 6.934209
#> unknown      1.988942 3.404334 6.906626

The fit gives d1 and d3 a positive association (an odds ratio of about 1.14), implied by their associations with d2, so the adjusted impacts differ from those with an odds ratio of 1. Unknown is not the same as independent; see vignette("interactions").

compare_methods() sets the model beside the published approximation:

compare_methods(m)
#> <cm_comparison> methods: published, deconflate
#> Impacts: milk yield loss
#> Units: % of yield
#> 
#> Adjusted values:
#>  disease raw published deconflate
#>       d1 2.5      2.07       2.14
#>       d2 5.0      3.70       3.39
#>       d3 7.5      6.75       6.93
#> 
#> Totals:
#>      method raw_sum adjusted_total
#>   published     2.5          2.111
#>  deconflate     2.5          2.109

The "published" column is the proportional approximation of Rasmussen et al. (2022, 2024), eq. 16. It is not a method of deconflate(): it is kept for comparison (compare_methods()) and for reproducing the published analyses (vignette("reproducing-published")) only. It is defined for one crude row per disease only.

The diagnostics report how well the adjusted impacts reconstruct the raw ones, the condition number of the conflation matrix, and adjusted impacts whose sign differs from the raw impact. A sign change means that the raw impact is smaller than the associated diseases alone would produce, so the inputs are inconsistent under the additive model (or the rows do not mean what they were taken to mean, e.g. an adjusted estimate entered as crude):

low_d2 <- cm_model(pop, cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(2.5, 0.2, 7.5)))
tryCatch(deconflate(low_d2), deconflate_sign_change = function(w) conditionMessage(w))
#> [1] "Adjusted impacts change sign for d2. The raw impacts are smaller than the associated diseases alone would produce under the additive model; check the estimates, and whether they come from populations with different comorbidity patterns."

Contributions

The expected aggregate impact per animal is sum_i p_i b_i (plus any interaction terms). Each disease’s contribution is its own term plus half of each interaction term it is involved in, which is its Shapley value in closed form. Contributions add up to the aggregate:

res$contributions
#>   disease      main interaction     total     share
#> 1      d1 0.2143250           0 0.2143250 0.1016130
#> 2      d2 0.5080619           0 0.5080619 0.2408757
#> 3      d3 1.3868419           0 1.3868419 0.6575113
res$totals
#>   raw_sum adjusted_total interaction_total
#> 1     2.5       2.109229                 0

raw_sum is the naive aggregate of the unadjusted impacts. The shares are NA when the aggregate is zero, since a share of zero is not defined. contribution_table() and summary() combine the impacts and contributions in one table.

How robust is a ranking or a sign to one uncertain input? cm_threshold() finds the input values at which the conclusion changes, for example the odds ratio of d2 and d3 at which d1 would contribute more than d2:

cm_threshold(m, "assoc:d2:d3", c(0.1, 100), conclusion = "rank")$thresholds[
  , c("item", "status", "threshold", "description")]
#>       item    status threshold                         description
#> 1 d1 vs d2 threshold  10.20365 d1 moves above d2 (by contribution)

See vignette("thresholds-and-scaling").

What an impact row means

An impact row is read as a crude or an adjusted estimate, depending on adjusted_for:

  • empty (the default): crude, the difference in the outcome between animals with and without the disease, not adjusted for other diseases;
  • disease ids separated by ";", or "all" for every other disease: adjusted, the coefficient of the disease in an additive (linear) regression of the outcome on the disease and those diseases.

Ids in adjusted_for that are not diseases of the model (herd, parity, …) are noted and otherwise ignored. For an adjusted estimate, the package uses the population regression implied by the distribution of disease combinations. This requires that the probabilities and associations describe the source population of the estimates. Other adjusted estimates (matched or propensity-score estimates, for example) are not supported.

A row can also be about a combination of diseases ("d1;d2": animals with both compared with animals with neither), which identifies an interaction, and it can hold within a subgroup (among, e.g. "d2", "no d2" or "no others" for animals with none of the other diseases). A disease can have several rows; when they have distributions, they are combined by weighted least squares and $heterogeneity says how well they agree. See ?cm_impacts and vignette("interactions").

A worked example: in the population above, the true additive impacts are 0.02, 0.04 and 0.06. A study of d1 that adjusted for d2, and crude studies of d2 and d3, would report:

truth <- c(d1 = 0.02, d2 = 0.04, d3 = 0.06)
raw <- simulate_raw_impacts(pop, truth, adjusted_for = c("d2", NA, NA))
round(raw$value, 4)
#> [1] 0.0187 0.0541 0.0667

With adjusted_for recorded, the adjustment recovers the truth:

imp_adj <- cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), raw$value, adjusted_for = c("d2", NA, NA))
m_adj <- cm_model(pop, imp_adj)
deconflate(m_adj)$adjusted
#>   disease    kind        raw adjusted      change rows
#> 1      d1 disease 0.01866481     0.02  0.07153525    1
#> 2      d2 disease 0.05406438     0.04 -0.26014129    1
#> 3      d3 disease 0.06668175     0.06 -0.10020359    1

Treating the d1 estimate as crude adjusts it a second time for d2 and gives the wrong answer:

m_wrong <- cm_model(pop, cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), imp_adj$value))
deconflate(m_wrong)$adjusted$adjusted
#> [1] 0.01440635 0.04043097 0.05992801

The published approximation is not defined for adjusted estimates; compare_methods() records the reason:

compare_methods(m_adj)$failed
#>                                                                                                                published 
#> "The published approximation is defined for one crude impact per disease (no combinations, subgroups or adjusted rows)."

Uncertainty

When inputs have distributions (the dist columns of the input tables, or distributions in cm_model()), deconflate() also draws them (n_draws = 1000 by default) and adds 95% intervals. The central estimate always uses the point values. Without distributions no draws are run, and a note says so (as in the results above). The five-disease example has distributions for most inputs; 200 draws keep this example fast:

res_five <- deconflate(five, n_draws = 200, seed = 1)
res_five
#> <cm_result> full model; milk yield loss [% of yield]
#> 
#>  disease raw adjusted  lower upper  change
#>      LAM 4.8    4.104 2.4028 5.655 -0.1451
#>      MAS 3.3    2.284 0.8229 4.393 -0.3078
#>      MET 5.6    4.520 2.4504 6.279 -0.1928
#>      SCK 2.5    1.381 0.7343 2.148 -0.4477
#>       RP 4.2    2.669 1.6092 3.299 -0.3646
#> 
#> Raw sum: 3.742; adjusted total: 2.713 (95% interval 2.179 to 3.578)
#> Diagnostics: residual 4.44e-16, condition number 1.79, sign changes 0
#> Pooled or over-determined items: 1 (see $heterogeneity and $estimates)
#> Uncertainty: 95% intervals from 200 draws (0 rejected; random sampling; seed 1).
#> 
#> Notes:
#> * Several association rows were pooled for 1 item (random effects; see
#>   $heterogeneity).

Pass n_draws = 0 for point estimates only. See vignette("uncertainty") for the draws, their stability checks and the sensitivity tools.

Event impacts

Impacts on the risk of an event, such as culling or death, are hazard ratios, rate ratios, risk ratios, odds ratios or risk differences rather than additive amounts. They are given with a measure (one per row; measures can be mixed), crude or adjusted as above, and adjusted with event_model = TRUE and the overall risk of the event over the period:

cull <- cm_model(pop, cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(1.5, 2.0, 1.2),
                                 measure = c("HR", "HR", "RR"), label = "culling"))
res_cull <- deconflate(cull, event_model = TRUE, overall_risk = 0.25)
res_cull$adjusted
#>   disease    kind measure raw adjusted      change rows
#> 1      d1 disease      HR 1.5 1.381707 -0.07886199    1
#> 2      d2 disease      HR 2.0 1.908294 -0.04585287    1
#> 3      d3 disease      RR 1.2 1.097741          NA    1
res_cull$attributable$summary
#>   overall_risk disease_free_risk attributable attributable_fraction
#> 1         0.25         0.2147648   0.03523521             0.1409408
#>    unallocated
#> 1 1.734723e-16

The adjusted values are each disease’s own hazard ratio, and $attributable gives the risk attributable to disease and its allocation to diseases. See vignette("event-impacts").

From adjusted impacts to gaps and values

deconflate() returns impacts and contributions in the units of the impacts; it does not convert them into other quantities. Turning them into a gap between the observed and the disease-free level of an outcome, or into a value, needs to know what the impacts mean, and takes a few lines of base R.

When the impacts are percentage losses relative to the disease-free level (as in m, with an observed mean of 10,000 units), the disease-free level is observed / (1 - aggregate / 100), the gap is the disease-free level minus the observed level, and each disease’s part of the gap is its share of the aggregate:

observed <- 10000
aggregate <- res$totals$adjusted_total            # in percent
disease_free <- observed / (1 - aggregate / 100)
gap <- disease_free - observed
ct <- res$contributions
by_disease <- data.frame(disease = ct$disease, gap = gap * ct$share)
by_disease
#>   disease       gap
#> 1      d1  21.89431
#> 2      d2  51.90090
#> 3      d3 141.67238
c(disease_free = disease_free, gap = gap)
#> disease_free          gap 
#>   10215.4676     215.4676

A value per unit of outcome turns the gaps into values; any costs that are not part of the adjustment are added separately:

unit_value <- 0.30
by_disease$value <- by_disease$gap * unit_value
sum(by_disease$value)
#> [1] 64.64028

ct$share is NA when the aggregate is zero; disease_free * ct$total / 100 gives the same gaps and stays defined. For an outcome that disease increases, the disease-free level is observed / (1 + aggregate / 100) and the gap is observed - disease_free. When the impacts are absolute effects (in the outcome’s own units, such as the days of the calving-interval model ci above), no conversion is needed: each disease’s contribution (ct$total) is its part of the gap, and the aggregate is the gap. With draws, the gap increases with the aggregate, so the same formula applied to the interval bounds of the aggregate (adjusted_total_lower and adjusted_total_upper in $totals) gives an interval for the total gap.

Feasibility

Each pairwise table can be valid on its own while no population has all of them. Fitting the distribution of disease combinations for the central estimate checks that the rows can hold together:

res$diagnostics$feasibility
#> [1] "joint distribution fitted (max residual 8.3e-12)"

Three diseases with probability 0.5, two strong positive associations and one strong negative one cannot coexist:

bad <- cm_model(
  cm_diseases(c("a", "b", "c"), c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5)),
  cm_impacts(c("a", "b", "c"), c(1, 2, 3)),
  associations = cm_associations(c("a", "a", "b"), c("b", "c", "c"), c(20, 20, 0.05))
)
check_feasibility(bad, method = "triples")
#> <cm_feasibility> NOT jointly feasible [triples]
#> 
#> Conflicting triples:
#>  disease1 disease2 disease3   gap
#>         a        b        c 0.226

check_feasibility() screens every triple of diseases (a necessary condition) and, with method = "lp", runs an exact check of the pairwise tables (it needs the lpSolve package).

Conditions

Errors and warnings have classes, so that callers (and the draws and sensitivity tools of the package) can handle them separately:

Class Meaning
deconflate_infeasible inputs that admit no valid probabilities (e.g. the example above)
deconflate_singular a singular or non-identifiable system
deconflate_nonconvergence a numerical procedure did not converge
deconflate_unsupported inputs or arguments that are not supported (or no longer used)
deconflate_nonfinite non-finite results
deconflate_input_problems cm_read_inputs() found errors in the input tables

All errors also have class deconflate_error, and warnings deconflate_warning (e.g. deconflate_sign_change).

e <- tryCatch(deconflate(bad), deconflate_error = function(e) e)
class(e)
#> [1] "deconflate_infeasible" "deconflate_error"      "error"                
#> [4] "condition"
conditionMessage(e)
#> [1] "The associations cannot all hold together: no population has all of them (conflicting triples: a-b-c). See check_feasibility()."

deconflate() also needs at least one association; without any, there is nothing to de-conflate (the diseases would be treated as independent), and it points to the tools that show how much associations could matter:

no_assoc <- cm_model(pop$diseases, yield)
tryCatch(deconflate(no_assoc), deconflate_error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "No association estimates were given, so there is nothing to de-conflate (the diseases would be treated as independent). To see how much associations could change the results, use screen_associations() or cm_threshold()."

Checking the method with a simulated herd

simulate_raw_impacts() computes the raw impacts that single-disease studies would report in a herd with known true impacts. Adjusting them should recover the truth; the published approximation (shown for comparison) does so only approximately:

m_sim <- cm_model(pop, simulate_raw_impacts(pop, c(d1 = 2, d2 = 4, d3 = 6)))
compare_methods(m_sim)
#> <cm_comparison> methods: published, deconflate
#> 
#> Adjusted values:
#>  disease  raw published deconflate
#>       d1 2.42      1.96          2
#>       d2 5.41      4.19          4
#>       d3 6.67      5.87          6
#> 
#> Totals:
#>      method raw_sum adjusted_total
#>   published   2.387          1.998
#>  deconflate   2.387          2.000
